explanation: Digital Data Discovery & Assessment is the capability to systematically identify, compare, and evaluate internal, administrative, external, and alternative data sources using standardized metadata, suitability criteria, and automated discovery tools. In future work, this supports leading needs analysis, prioritizing reusable digital assets before proposing new surveys, and ensuring processing and analysis designs are built around machine-actionable, FAIR, and automation-ready data inputs.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the current work description does not explicitly require expertise in digital data discovery, suitability assessment frameworks, or automated source evaluation, yet these are becoming essential to future work. This need is driven by the Mandate letters’ expectation for modernized, efficient, and lower-burden data approaches, the Departmental Plan’s emphasis on digital transformation, administrative and alternative data use, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide direction to prioritize automated discovery, enterprise-wide triage, and standardized, metadata-driven decision-making before new collection is approved.

explanation: Automation Readiness Assessment is the capability to systematically determine whether a statistical program or business process can be supported by automation, alternative data, or reusable digital workflows before new collection or manual approaches are pursued. It includes applying standardized feasibility criteria across needs identification, data availability and suitability checks, and processing design so decisions are auditable, scalable, and aligned with enterprise digital priorities.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Departmental Plan, Mandate letters, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide requires leaders to prioritize digital-first, automated, and reusable solutions when identifying needs, assessing available data, and designing processing and analysis workflows. The change to work makes automation feasibility assessment a core operational requirement: sub-divisional programs must use standardized frameworks to evaluate internal, administrative, and alternative data options, document why new surveys are necessary, and ensure processes are designed for modular automation, interoperability, and auditability.

skill_gap: Cost-Benefit and Tradeoff Analysis in Digital Context
explanation: This capability enables leaders to assess whether a data need should be met through existing digital, administrative, alternative, or automated sources before recommending a new survey. It requires interpreting structured cost-benefit and tradeoff analysis across timeliness, quality, reuse, risk, and strategic alignment so that survey initiation becomes an evidence-based exception rather than the default.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future-state work described in GSBPM 1.1, 1.2, and 1.5 requires a mandatory digital-first pre-assessment, explicit tradeoff analysis, and documented justification before any new survey proceeds, while the current approval process does not include cost-benefit analysis or digital-asset pre-screening. This directly reflects the change drivers in the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide, which collectively push the organization toward greater use of administrative and alternative data, automation, efficiency, transparency, and strategic prioritization in how new data needs are assessed.

skill_gap: Enterprise Data Asset Reuse & Digital Feasibility Planning
explanation: This capability is the ability to assess whether business needs can be met by reusing existing enterprise data assets, integrating across programs, and prioritizing scalable digital solutions before launching new collection or bespoke projects. It supports stronger upfront planning, resource allocation, and contract decisions by requiring staff to evaluate data availability, digital feasibility, interoperability, and long-term reuse potential across the organization.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Departmental Plan, Mandate letters, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide requires more coordinated, digital-first, and enterprise-wide decision-making on how data needs are met. The change drivers directly influence GSBPM 1.1, 1.5, and 5.1 by expecting staff to identify needs through enterprise asset scanning, verify data availability through automated and metadata-driven discovery, and plan for interoperable integration at scale—yet there is currently no explicit capability requirement for cross-program data asset reuse and digital feasibility analysis.

skill_gap: Digital Feasibility Communication & Business Case Defense
explanation: This capability is the ability to communicate, in clear business terms, why a proposed survey or project is necessary after existing data assets, alternative sources, automation options, and modular approaches have been systematically assessed. It includes presenting evidence-based trade-offs on cost, time, risk, capacity, and strategic fit, and defending recommendations during needs identification, data availability assessment, and business case approval.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described across GSBPM 1.1, 1.5, and 1.6 requires staff not only to perform digital-first and automation-first assessments, but to clearly explain and defend those findings in governance and approval processes, while no explicit communication requirement currently exists. This is directly driven by Mandate letters emphasizing efficient, modern digital government, the Departmental Plan’s focus on enterprise alignment, automation, and responsible resource use, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide’s expectation that existing data, alternative sources, and automated solutions be exhausted and transparently justified before new survey collection proceeds.

explanation: This capability is the ability to use automated asset review and assessment tools to identify, compare, and evaluate existing data assets through machine-actionable metadata, standardized rules, and suitability scoring. It supports faster concept identification, data availability checks, and validation by making asset discovery more exhaustive, evidence-based, and reusable, while reserving human effort for complex cases, risk assessment, and governance.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide points to more transparent, evidence-driven decisions on whether new initiatives or surveys are justified, with existing assets assessed first through automated tools. These change drivers directly influence work in GSBPM 1.4, 1.5, and 5.3 by requiring staff to work with AI-enabled discovery platforms, machine-actionable metadata, and automated review and validation processes that are not currently emphasized to the needed level.

skill_gap: Cost-benefit & Feasibility Analysis in Asset Reuse
explanation: This capability is the ability to quickly assess whether existing internal, administrative, or alternative data assets can meet a need before proposing new collection, using cost-benefit, feasibility, quality, timeliness, and reusability criteria. In practice, it supports evidence-based consultations and needs identification by helping staff use metadata, automated discovery tools, and structured decision rules to compare options, justify exceptions, and negotiate the best-fit solution with stakeholders.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Departmental Plan and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide shifts the organization from a survey-first model to a reuse-first, digitally enabled model where existing data assets must be systematically assessed before new surveys are considered. It is also reinforced by Mandate letters emphasizing efficiency, reduced burden, and better use of existing data, making cost-benefit and feasibility analysis essential in GSBPM 1.1, 1.2, and 1.5 to support rapid consultation, transparent decision-making, and strong evidence-based justification for any new collection.

explanation: Stakeholder dialogue platforms are the digital tools and practices used to run structured, transparent consultations with clients, partners, and data owners when identifying needs and assessing whether existing data assets can meet them. This capability supports faster, evidence-based discussions using searchable metadata, dashboards, and decision logs so staff can compare options, weigh trade-offs, and justify when new survey collection is truly necessary.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in GSBPM 1.1, 1.2, and 1.5 requires staff to engage stakeholders through machine-actionable metadata platforms, agile consultation cycles, and transparent cost-benefit discussions before proposing new surveys. This directly reflects the change drivers in Mandate letters, the Departmental Plan, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide, which push the organization toward digital-first, asset-based, reusable, and evidence-driven decision-making; however, the current description does not explicitly cover capability with platforms that enable and document this new form of stakeholder engagement.

explanation: Transparent Evidence-based Advocacy is the capability to guide stakeholder discussions and negotiations using clear evidence from asset reviews, metadata-driven data discovery, cost-benefit analysis, and reuse potential before proposing new collection. In future work across identifying needs, consulting stakeholders, and checking data availability, employees must quickly explain trade-offs, document rationale transparently, and build strong business cases showing why a new survey is necessary only when existing or alternative sources are insufficient.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively push the organization toward greater reuse of existing data, stronger transparency in decision-making, reduced unnecessary collection, and more digital, automated, and accountable workflows. These change drivers directly influence future work in GSBPM 1.1, 1.2, and 1.5 by requiring staff to justify new surveys through explicit evidence, cost-benefit and impact analysis, and transparent negotiation grounded in asset reviews, legal/privacy context, and strategic fit.

explanation: Machine-readable metadata synthesis is the ability to interpret and combine standardized, machine-actionable metadata so staff can quickly identify suitable data assets, align concepts to existing standards, and design automated, reusable processing and analysis workflows. This capability supports asset-first decision-making by enabling systematic data discovery, metadata-driven suitability assessment, and evidence-based justification when proposing new surveys.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the current work description does not explicitly include the ability to synthesize and apply machine-actionable metadata, yet this is becoming essential to future work under GSBPM 1.4, 1.5, and 2.5. The Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively drive greater use of existing data assets, automation, FAIR metadata, and standardized digital workflows, which in turn require staff to use metadata to assess data availability, support concept alignment, and justify survey design only when no suitable asset exists.

explanation: Enterprise Automation Frameworks is the capability to understand and apply automation strategies, workflow orchestration approaches, and reusable digital design patterns in statistical operations. It enables staff to assess automation readiness, design modular and auditable production workflows, and configure standardized, metadata-driven processes that reduce manual intervention while supporting scalability, compliance, and cross-program reuse.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively point to a digital-first, interoperable, and adaptive operating model in which statistical work must be designed for automation, reuse, and rapid iteration. Those change drivers directly influence future work requirements in GSBPM 2.6, 3.4, and 8.3 by requiring production systems, workflow configuration, and action planning to be modular, version-controlled, traceable, and increasingly supported by automated platforms, self-service tools, and real-time monitoring.

explanation: Digital Transformation Leadership is the capability to lead teams in redesigning statistical program operations so workflows are digital-first, automation-ready, and built for data reuse, interoperability, and auditability. In practice, this means directing work so needs identification, processing design, and production workflow design are standardized, metadata-driven, modular, and machine-actionable, with close collaboration across business, IT, and data engineering functions.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the change drivers in the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively require leaders to embed digital workflow, interoperability, automation, and reuse considerations into core program decisions and approvals. These drivers directly influence future work requirements in GSBPM 1.1, 2.5, and 2.6 by shifting expectations from managing traditional manual operations to leading configurable, version-controlled, AI-enabled, and cross-program production environments.

explanation: Digital-Era Cost-Benefit Analysis is the capability to build business cases that systematically compare existing data, administrative and alternative sources, automation, interoperability, and reusable enterprise solutions against manual processes or new survey collection. It supports earlier, evidence-based decisions in identifying needs, checking data availability and suitability, and preparing business cases by requiring transparent analysis of cost, risk, scalability, strategic fit, and expected outcomes before proposing bespoke or survey-based approaches.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively drive a shift toward digital delivery, enterprise platforms, automation, reuse of data assets, and faster, more transparent governance decisions. These change drivers directly influence future work in GSBPM 1.1, 1.5, and 1.6 by requiring staff to assess interoperable and automated options first, document why new collection is necessary, and justify approvals and funding through formal cost-benefit cases aligned with agency-wide digital priorities.

explanation: Data Source Integration and Interoperability is the capability to identify, assess, and combine internal, administrative, and external data sources using common standards, reusable metadata, and interoperable digital processes. In practice, it enables staff to evaluate existing data first, configure auditable integration pipelines, and support rapid, scalable data blending with minimal manual effort across needs identification, data availability assessment, and data integration activities.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively drive a shift toward digital-first, interoperable, and cost-effective statistical production, where existing data reuse and automation must be considered before launching new surveys. These change drivers directly influence future work requirements in GSBPM 1.1, 1.5, and 5.1 by requiring enterprise-wide data discovery, evidence-based suitability assessment, and standardized, AI-enabled integration approaches grounded in strong cost-benefit and digital execution expectations.

explanation: Digital Delivery and Automation-Readiness is the capability to plan statistical work so digital-first, automated, and reusable solutions are built in from the start. It includes understanding the skills, technologies, contracts, governance, and resource choices needed to support standardized data discovery, metadata-driven design, modular processing, and automated output pipelines across activities such as identifying needs, designing processing and analysis, and preparing draft outputs.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively drive future work toward modernized, digital-first, efficient, and scalable statistical operations. These change drivers influence requirements in GSBPM 1.1, 2.5, and 6.1 by making automation compatibility, interoperable design, reusable workflows, and auditable automated outputs essential considerations in planning, staffing, project design, and budget decisions.

explanation: Digital Data Asset Evaluation is the capability to assess whether internal, administrative, alternative, and external digital data sources are suitable, lawful, high quality, and machine-actionable before proposing new collection. It supports needs identification, data availability assessment, and processing design by requiring staff to use standardized metadata, automated discovery and suitability screening, and evidence-based business cases so surveys and manual collection are used only when no viable reusable data source exists.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively drive a shift toward digital-first, reusable, automated, and lower-burden data production. Those change drivers influence future work requirements in GSBPM 1.1, 1.5, and 2.5 by requiring staff to prioritize existing data assets, document why new collection is necessary, and design metadata-driven, auditable, automation-compatible workflows that incorporate legal, privacy, quality, and operational feasibility assessments.

explanation: Enterprise Metadata Analysis is the capability to assess, validate, and interpret AI-generated concepts, metadata, and system recommendations within enterprise digital environments. It enables staff to confirm suitability, resolve exceptions, and ensure concepts, data sources, and processing rules align with enterprise standards, FAIR principles, and automated workflows across concept identification, data suitability assessment, and processing design.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Departmental Plan and StatCan 2030 Future Slide points to more automated, metadata-driven, and standardized statistical operations, while Mandate letters reinforce expectations for digital modernization, efficiency, and responsible use of data and technology. These change drivers shift work away from manual concept creation and review toward validating machine-suggested concepts, assessing automated suitability results, and supporting auditable, machine-actionable processing designs, creating a clear need for stronger enterprise metadata analysis capability.

explanation: Policy Negotiation and Justification is the capability to clearly explain, defend, and negotiate decisions about concept alignment when AI tools recommend standardized concepts, data sources, or design options. As concept identification and data suitability checks become more automated, staff will need to validate machine-generated recommendations, resolve conflicts across programs, and provide strong, evidence-based rationale when proposing exceptions to enterprise standards.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide all point toward greater standardization, automation, faster delivery, and stronger enterprise governance in statistical production. These change drivers directly influence future work in GSBPM 1.4, 1.5, and 6.3 by making AI-suggested concepts and data options the default, requiring employees to justify departures through transparent governance processes, negotiate with stakeholders and data partners, and clearly explain decisions, risks, and limitations in high-throughput, AI-enabled workflows.

explanation: Digital arbitration and conflict resolution is the ability to quickly mediate disagreements among program, methodology, disclosure, and digital teams when AI tools suggest concepts, standards, or dissemination approaches. As concept identification, output design, and disclosure control become more automated and metadata-driven, employees must resolve competing priorities in fast, platform-enabled workflows while maintaining alignment, compliance, and trust.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide all point toward faster digital delivery, greater automation, stronger standardization, and increased use of AI-enabled platforms across the statistical production process. These change drivers directly influence future work in GSBPM 1.4, 2.1, and 6.4 by compressing timelines, increasing cross-functional decision points, and requiring staff to arbitrate quickly on AI-generated concepts, machine-actionable outputs, and embedded disclosure rules so work can proceed efficiently and consistently.

explanation: Digital platform integration is the capability to ensure statistical concepts and metadata are consistently structured, aligned, and governed across enterprise digital platforms and architectures. It enables staff to work beyond subject-matter expertise by configuring interoperable components, applying metadata standards, and supporting auditable, automated data integration and concept reuse across the statistical production process.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in GSBPM 5.1, 1.2, and 1.4 requires staff to embed concepts within AI-enabled, interoperable, and governed digital ecosystems rather than manage them only within individual programs. This direction is driven by the Mandate letters’ emphasis on modern, digital government, the Departmental Plan’s focus on enterprise data and service modernization, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide’s vision for reusable, standardized, FAIR-enabled platforms, all of which increase the need for knowledge of digital architectures, metadata governance, and platform-based integration.

explanation: This capability is the ability to critically evaluate AI-generated concepts and conceptual frameworks, confirm their methodological soundness, and determine whether they are appropriate for use in statistical research and analysis. As concept identification, data suitability screening, and analytical interpretation become more automated, employees will need to focus less on creating concepts from scratch and more on validating AI suggestions, resolving conflicts, ensuring alignment with standards, and explaining the quality, limits, and practical implications of AI-supported outputs.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide all point toward greater use of automation, AI, standardized metadata, and faster end-to-end production of data and analytical products. These change drivers directly influence future work in GSBPM 1.4, 1.5, and 6.3 by shifting staff responsibilities toward human oversight, quality assurance, ethical and methodological validation, and contextual interpretation of AI-generated concepts and outputs, exposing a clear gap in the ability to assess the suitability and implications of AI-derived conceptual frameworks.

explanation: This capability is the ability to understand, oversee, and troubleshoot automated tools that scan internal, administrative, and alternative data sources to determine whether existing data can meet a need before a new survey is considered. It supports future work in needs identification and data availability assessment by enabling staff to interpret suitability scores, metadata-driven recommendations, and decision rules, while intervening only in complex legal, ethical, quality, or partner-management cases. It also connects to collection design by ensuring that new survey instruments are pursued only when automated evidence shows no suitable reusable or extractable source exists.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future-state work described in the Departmental Plan, Mandate letters, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide emphasizes reducing unnecessary collection, increasing use of administrative and alternative data, and expanding automation and digital decision-making. Those change drivers shift work away from routine survey operations toward enterprise-wide data discovery, automated suitability screening, and evidence-based justification for rare survey launches, making it essential for managers and staff to understand how these tools operate and how their outputs shape downstream decisions in GSBPM 1.1, 1.5, and 3.1.

skill_gap: Multidisciplinary Team Management in Technology-Enabled Settings
explanation: This capability is the ability to lead multidisciplinary teams across technology, legal, data science, and subject-matter domains in environments where data discovery, suitability assessment, and collection design are increasingly automated and metadata-driven. It requires coordinating shared decisions on when existing or alternative data sources can meet needs, when human review is required for complex legal or ethical cases, and when rare survey collection should proceed based on strong evidence and enterprise priorities.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Departmental Plan and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide shifts activity in GSBPM 1.1, 1.5, and 2.3 away from routine survey operations toward automated needs triage, exhaustive data-source evaluation, and AI-enabled collection design. In line with Mandate letters emphasizing digital modernization, responsible data use, and integrated service delivery, leaders will need to oversee automated vetting processes and align diverse specialists to make defensible, high-stakes decisions on data acquisition, compliance, risk, and exceptional survey launches.

skill_gap: Interpretation of Machine-Actionable Metadata and Suitability Logic
explanation: This capability is the ability to interpret machine-actionable metadata, automated suitability scores, and decision rules to determine whether existing data sources can meet a need and to translate those results into clear, evidence-based recommendations. As work shifts toward automated discovery, screening, and AI-supported analysis, employees must explain technical outputs in plain language, assess legal, ethical, and quality implications, and support transparent decisions on when a new survey is truly necessary.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future-state direction in Mandate letters, the Departmental Plan, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide points to greater use of administrative and alternative data, automation, FAIR-aligned metadata, and responsible AI-enabled decision-making. These change drivers reshape work in GSBPM 1.5, 2.5, and 6.3 by making automated suitability assessment and metadata-driven workflows the default, while increasing the need for staff who can interpret system outputs, justify exceptions with transparent evidence, and communicate implications to non-technical stakeholders.

skill_gap: Advanced Legal and Ethical Risk Assessment
explanation: Advanced Legal and Ethical Risk Assessment is the capability to evaluate the legal, privacy, and ethical implications of using integrated administrative, alternative, and automated data sources, and to guide decisions with clear, defensible evidence. As data availability checks, needs identification, and validation become increasingly automated, staff must focus on high-risk exceptions, assess whether proposed data use is appropriate and compliant, and support negotiations and oversight where no straightforward data alternative exists.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Departmental Plan, Mandate letters, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide shifts effort away from routine survey design toward automated data discovery, reuse of existing data, and transparent justification for any new collection. These change drivers increase the importance of legal, privacy, and ethical review in GSBPM activities 1.1, 1.5, and 5.3, where staff must interpret automated suitability results, manage complex risk cases, and ensure technology-enabled decisions remain compliant, auditable, and aligned with public trust expectations.

skill_gap: Evidence-based Argumentation for Exceptional Data Collection
explanation: This capability is the ability to use automated assessments, metadata, and auditable decision outputs to build clear, defensible cases for when a new survey is truly necessary. In future collection design and data availability checks, staff will need to validate AI-supported evidence, show that existing and alternative data sources were systematically exhausted, and present transparent justification to support exceptional survey launches and related negotiations.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide all reinforce a shift toward modernized, transparent, and efficient data collection that prioritizes reuse of existing, administrative, and alternative data before launching new surveys. Across GSBPM 1.5, 2.3, and 3.1, these change drivers increase the need for staff to defend survey proposals with system-generated, auditable evidence, directly shaping future work toward exception-based survey design, higher-stakes negotiations, and stronger validation of automated outputs.

explanation: Complex Data Partnership Negotiation is the capability to secure access to administrative and private-sector data through high-stakes, multi-party negotiations where legal, ethical, privacy, and public-interest considerations must be balanced. As needs identification, consultation, and data availability checks become more automated and evidence-driven, staff must be able to use auditable suitability assessments to justify why external data access is required, resolve complex edge cases, and build trusted relationships with data holders when surveys are treated as a last resort.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in GSBPM 1.1, 1.2, and 1.5 shifts the organization toward automated data discovery, stricter justification for new surveys, and greater reliance on administrative and alternative data partnerships in complex cases. This aligns with the change drivers in the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide, which collectively emphasize modernization, reduced response burden, digital-first decision-making, and expanded use of existing and external data sources—thereby increasing the need for advanced negotiation capability to secure access and defend evidence-based survey decisions.

skill_gap: Data Sharing Agreements and Privacy Law
explanation: This capability is the ability to apply privacy law, data-sharing legislation, and agreement negotiation in operational environments where data discovery, suitability assessment, and integration are increasingly automated and metadata-driven. It includes judging whether data can be reused, shared, processed, and integrated within legal and ethical boundaries, while working with technical teams to embed privacy, disclosure, and access requirements into standardized workflows and machine-actionable processes.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide requires greater use of administrative and alternative data, stronger data sharing, and more automated, interoperable, privacy-preserving operations. Across GSBPM 1.5, 2.5, and 5.1, staff must assess legal suitability of data sources, design privacy and disclosure controls into automated processing, and manage complex integration and partner agreements, making combined legal, technical, and subject-matter knowledge essential.

skill_gap: Evaluation of Automated Data Availability Assessments
explanation: This capability is the ability to interpret and challenge the results of automated data discovery and suitability assessments to determine whether existing internal, administrative, or alternative data can meet a need before proposing new collection. It requires staff to use standardized metadata, system-generated evidence, and documented decision rules to confirm that automated checks are sufficient, identify edge cases, and support transparent, audit-ready recommendations.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Departmental Plan and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide shifts needs identification, data availability checks, and evaluation inputs toward automated, metadata-driven, and evidence-based workflows, especially in GSBPM 1.1, 1.5, and 8.1. It is also reinforced by Mandate letter expectations to reduce response burden, improve efficiency, and make better use of existing and alternative data, which means staff must be able to assess automated outputs rigorously and justify any new survey only when system evidence shows no suitable source exists.

explanation: This capability is the ability to assess needs, design options, and build recommendations using an automation-first lens—prioritizing reusable enterprise data, administrative and alternative sources, and modular, interoperable solutions before proposing new survey collection. It also includes constructing clear business cases grounded in cost-benefit, risk, reusability, and platform alignment, while supporting reproducible, auditable workflows across needs identification, component reuse, and business case development.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Departmental Plan, Mandate letters, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide requires EC-08 roles to move beyond survey optimization toward enterprise-wide, automation-compatible, and evidence-based decision-making. The change drivers point directly to future expectations in GSBPM 1.1, 3.2, and 1.6: scanning existing data assets first, championing modular reusable components, and submitting business cases that explicitly justify non-survey, automated, and platform-aligned approaches while discontinuing or iterating options that do not perform.
